title: How CPR Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the basics of CPR, starting with an urging to take a certified CPR class (American Heart Association, heart.org). They distinguish sudden cardiac arrest from heart attack, explain the sinoatrial node's role in heart rhythm, and describe how defibrillators work (they stop the heart so it can reset). They cover the history of resuscitation (Elisha in the Bible, 1740 Paris Academy recommendation of mouth-to-mouth for drowning, 1891 chest compressions by Dr. Frederick Maass, Dr. George Crile's 1904 report, Peter Safar and James Elam, 1960s CPR development). They walk through checking responsiveness, the 2010 switch from ABC to CAB, hands-only CPR for untrained rescuers, compression depth and rate (one to two inches, about 100 per minute, hummed to "Staying Alive"), infant CPR, moving a victim safely, Good Samaritan laws, and the low rate of bystander CPR in low-income neighborhoods. A listener mail from Dan in Austin describes his 16-year-old daughter's sudden cardiac arrest and recommends cardiac screening for children, citing Championship Hearts Foundation.

segments.title: Opening banter and CPR class plug
segments.summary: The hosts open the show and urge listeners to get certified in CPR through the American Heart Association's heart.org, noting this episode is not a substitute for a real class.

segments.title: Sudden cardiac arrest vs. heart attack
segments.summary: The sinoatrial node sets the heart's rhythm. When it goes haywire, the heart stops pumping effectively, causing sudden cardiac arrest, which differs from a heart attack that develops slowly. Survival odds for sudden cardiac arrest are about five percent.

segments.title: How defibrillators work
segments.summary: A defibrillator delivers a shock that turns the heart off so it can reset to a normal rhythm, rather than restarting it. Users should be trained before using one.

segments.title: History of CPR
segments.summary: Early resuscitation history: the Elisha Bible account, the 1740 Paris Academy recommendation of mouth-to-mouth for drowning, 1891 chest compressions by Dr. Frederick Maass, Dr. George Crile's 1904 report, and Peter Safar and James Elam's modern CPR in the 1950s and 1960s.

segments.title: Checking a victim and choosing CPR type
segments.summary: Check responsiveness and breathing, and roll a victim onto a firm surface while protecting the neck. Untrained rescuers should do hands-only CPR; trained but rusty rescuers should still lean toward hands-only; trained and confident rescuers can do full CPR with breaths. The 2010 change moved from ABC to CAB, and pulse checks were dropped for rescuers.

segments.title: Chest compression technique and infant CPR
segments.summary: Adults: heel of hand in center of chest between nipples, elbows locked, compress one to two inches at about 100 per minute, with 'Staying Alive' suggested as a tempo guide. Infants: two fingers, about one and a half inches, same rate, supporting the head. Compressions circulate oxygenated blood rather than restart the heart; rescue breathing adds oxygen.

segments.title: Good Samaritan laws, disease risk, and CPR disparities
segments.summary: Good Samaritan laws protect voluntary rescuers, with some states extending protection to untrained helpers. Disease transmission from mouth-to-mouth is considered rare. Freakonomics data show bystander CPR is less common in low-income and some Black neighborhoods. Hosts discuss fear and panic as barriers.

segments.title: Listener mail: Dan in Austin on pediatric sudden cardiac arrest
segments.summary: Dan writes that his healthy sixteen-year-old daughter died of sudden cardiac arrest while playing in their backyard. He urges screening for children and recommends Championship Hearts Foundation, which offers low-cost cardiac screening in Central Texas.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to heart.org for CPR courses and give contact info for submitting stories.
